The code is only
part of the work.

I’m Victor Mendivil. I work on software that has to make sense to the people using it—not just to the person who wrote it.

My experience is grounded in Dynamics 365 Finance & Operations and ERP. That means listening to requirements, shaping technical designs, implementing changes and carrying them through testing, deployment and support.

I care about the connections between those stages. A clear requirement helps a test mean something. A considered deployment helps a change become usable. Support brings the next questions back into the design.

Read about my approach
A little more
than a job title.

I like making complicated things understandable—and finding out how they work in the first place.

Outside my professional work, that curiosity turns toward Raspberry Pi, homelab servers and AI-assisted work processes and web applications. This collection gives those interests room without dressing them up as a list of accomplishments.

Working together

I’m employed full-time. Freelance conversations are best suited to contained needs for individuals or small businesses, with remote, evening or asynchronous collaboration discussed up front. Scope and availability need an honest conversation before any commitment.

Career conversations

I’m also interested in senior and technical-lead roles. That is a separate conversation from freelance work: one about responsibility, collaboration and the next step in my software practice.

From requirement
to workable system.

An illustrated reflection on software craft: understanding the need, making a change and staying responsible for what follows.

Personal practice essay / Illustrative artwork / Not a client case study

Intent into operation. Original artwork representing the passage from a written need to something people can use.
Start with the
actual need.

A request often arrives as a desired change: add a field, adjust a process, make a report. I want to understand what that change is meant to help someone do. Who uses the information? Where does it come from? What would a useful result look like?

In Dynamics 365 F&O and ERP work, those questions connect software to an existing way of operating. Requirements need to be specific enough for technical decisions, but also understandable enough for people from different teams to challenge them.

That is why I see clarification as part of development, not as a delay before it begins. The point is not to generate more documentation. It is to give the work a shared meaning.

Design it.
Build it.
Make it usable.

Requirements → technical design → implementation → testing → deployment → support.

This is a chain of responsibilities, not a claim that every project follows a perfect straight line.

Carry the context
with the change.

Technical design turns a need into choices. Implementation gives those choices a concrete form. Testing asks whether the result fits the original intention, including the less convenient paths that a happy-path demonstration can miss.

Deployment and support belong to that same story. A change is not finished merely because it works on a developer’s machine. People need to understand what changed, and the next person working on it needs enough context to make a considered decision.

Cross-team coordination helps that context survive. My approach is to connect the requirement, the implementation and the conversations around both—not to treat code as an isolated deliverable.

After-hours
curiosity.

Raspberry Pi, homelab servers and the appeal of understanding the parts for yourself.

Personal interests / Illustrative hardware / No project or performance claims

An imagined small machine, drawn for this edition. Not a photograph of my homelab or a particular Raspberry Pi model.
A smaller place
to ask questions.

A small computer can make a large topic feel approachable. My interest in Raspberry Pi and homelab servers is about that opportunity: looking beneath the application and considering the machine, the network and the responsibilities around them.

What has to stay running? Which parts depend on each other? What would I need to know if something stopped responding? These are useful questions even when the setting is personal rather than a production system.

This page is an expression of that curiosity, not a documented build log. The hardware image is an original illustration; it should not be read as evidence of equipment I own or a configuration I have deployed.

There is a particular pleasure in making room for a question you don’t yet know how to answer.

Curiosity connects
back to craft.

Software depends on more than software. A personal server is a way to think about those surrounding layers: how a service starts, where information lives, and what maintenance asks of the person responsible for it.

I do not need to turn every interest into a polished case study. Some explorations matter because they make the next technical conversation better informed. That is the spirit of this edition.

Tools,
with judgment.

AI-assisted processes and web apps interest me. The responsibility for understanding the result does not disappear.

Personal approach / Illustrative edition / No benchmark or delivery claims

Original typographic artwork: assistance and accountability are not opposites.
A helpful tool
is still a tool.

AI can be a way to explore a problem, shape an initial idea or ask for a different explanation. I’m interested in AI-assisted work processes and web applications for those possibilities—not because a generated answer automatically becomes a reliable one.

The interesting question is where assistance fits. What is the task? What context does the tool have? What needs an independent check? Those questions keep the person doing the work in the picture.

Speed does not
replace a check.

A plausible answer can still be wrong. In software work, the result needs to be read, understood and exercised. I want assistance to support that process, not to become an excuse for skipping it.

For an illustrative example, imagine asking a tool to outline a small web-app feature. Its suggestions could help identify options. The developer still has to decide what belongs in scope, inspect the implementation and test the actual behavior. This is a thought experiment, not an account of a delivered client project.

My interest is in a useful relationship with the tool: ask clearly, inspect carefully, test what matters and own the result. That principle connects this newer curiosity to the rest of my software practice.
